 Proposed federal changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program could cause some Michigan families to lose food assistance, prompting advocates to warn that the program is “a really crucial safety net.”
 The Save My SNAP coalition is speaking out after proposed changes were introduced that would reduce eligibility for people who receive SNAP. The proposal would change “categorical eligibility,” meaning some people who received Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, also known as TANF, would lose SNAP benefits.
 Under the proposal, some households with gross incomes slightly above 130 percent of the poverty line would lose SNAP benefits. The Trump administration said the proposed changes would “ensure that SNAP benefits are targeted to needy households.”
 “This is all against a really dire backdrop for SNAP,” said Elinor Jordan, a public benefits attorney at the Michigan Poverty Law Program and a co-chair of the Save My SNAP coalition. “The Save My SNAP coalition was formed because SNAP is at a crossroads right now. Over 150,000 Michiganders have already lost SNAP over the past year or so due to federal policy changes.”
 Jordan said the impact would be felt statewide. “This is affecting people in rural areas and urban areas in upper Michigan, southern Michigan, all over the state,” she said.
 According to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, 6 million people would be impacted by the change. Organization Vice President Ty Jones Cox said certain families would lose access to SNAP, including a family of three making $35,000 a year.
 Jordan also raised concerns about how the proposed changes could affect the state’s administration of the program. “Over 150,000 Michiganders have already lost SNAP over the past year or so due to federal policy changes,” she said. “And so we’re worried that these rule changes, adding to administrative costs, could create a higher error rate, punishing the state even more.”
 Jordan said if the change happens, it will also affect food banks, which are already seeing long lines. She also said she is concerned about how the proposal could affect domestic violence survivors who rely on food assistance.
 “I work with legal aid across Michigan, and our legal services attorneys regularly work with survivors who are really relying on things like SNAP benefits to give them enough financial wherewithal to leave a dangerous relationship,” Jordan said. “And so this kind of burden on a domestic violence survivor not being able to be as easily eligible for SNAP is highly problematic.”
 The change is still only proposed. The administration must allow 30 days for public comment , and it will receive written comments on or before Dec. 10.
